evals.prompt: I need to add a notification system to our app. Users should get email and in-app notifications when someone comments on their posts. We're using a Node.js/Express backend with PostgreSQL and a React frontend. Can you help me plan this out?
evals.expected_output: This prompt names the stack, the user, and the target behavior, so Step 1's draft branch applies: the reply states its open questions AND carries the full plan in the same response — acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then format, 5-10 granular tasks with dependencies, and risk identification. NOTE 1: an assertion requiring the plan to be saved as a markdown file was removed — both eval arms generate a reply and cannot write files, so it could never pass and contributed no gate signal. Verify file creation in a real session instead. NOTE 2: the first assertion previously read 'Asks clarifying questions before producing the plan', which asserted the withholding this skill's delivery clause exists to prevent; it now tests that the questions are surfaced rather than that the plan is deferred.
assertions: Surfaces its open questions or the assumptions it is planning under, rather than silently assuming
Includes acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then format
Tasks are granular (1-4 hours each) with clear deliverables
Dependency map is present showing task ordering
Risks section identifies at least 2 technical risks
Out of scope section explicitly excludes something

evals.prompt: plan adding dark mode to our vue app
evals.expected_output: The ask-first branch of Step 1: the request names no concrete behavior, persistence, or theming approach, so the reply asks before drafting (CSS variables vs theme library? System preference detection? Per-component or global? Persistence?) and says what it would need to start drafting. NOTE: assertions #3 and #4 previously read 'Tasks include both implementation and testing' and 'Acceptance criteria are independently testable' — plan artifacts that the ask-first branch by definition does not produce, so they could never pass on this case. They now test the coverage of the clarification itself. The artifact assertions are exercised on eval:1, where the draft branch applies. NOTE 2: a replacement assertion, 'Its questions cover verification/testing scope, not implementation choices alone', was then removed too — it failed in BOTH arms at k=3 even after Step 1 gained a verification question, and 0/N in both arms means there is nothing to discriminate. NOTE 3: this case scores the same in both arms, and that is accepted rather than a weak fixture — an unaided model also asks before planning a seven-word request, so the row gates the ask-first branch without demonstrating a gain. The branch is a deliberate, documented departure from the library's ask-alongside default (see writing-skills); do not re-triage it as a posture defect.
assertions: Does not immediately produce a plan from this vague request
Applies YAGNI by not over-engineering the approach
Names what it would need in order to start drafting the plan

evals.prompt: We've committed to building SSO for enterprise customers — SAML plus SCIM provisioning, with admin-managed roles. Sales has already told two prospects it lands next quarter. Break it up for the team, and tell me whether next quarter is real.
evals.expected_output: The request asks for two things the roster does not separate. Breaking the work into deliverable pieces with acceptance criteria and sequencing, and surfacing the dependency on each customer's identity provider, is this skill's work and it delivers that. Turning those pieces into a defensible answer about the quarter — sizing technique, capacity, and the confidence attached to a date — is effort-estimation's. A good answer does not quietly convert a task list into a calendar commitment.
assertions: Separates the two halves: breaking the work into deliverable pieces, versus deciding how much calendar those pieces add up to
Refers to effort-estimation for sizing the work and testing the next-quarter date against team capacity
Delivers the breakdown itself — scoped tasks with acceptance criteria — rather than deferring the whole request
Identifies the dependency outside the team's control, such as each customer's identity provider
